target.text: Me pone un cortado, por favor

mnemonic.title: Cortado Porcelain Tap
mnemonic.text: Tap a teaspoon on the cup on each stressed syllable: me PO-ne un cor-TA-do, por fa-VOR.

grammar.title: «Me pone...» Courtesy Formula
grammar.text: Unlike the stiff imperative «Póngame» or English "Give me", native Spanish speakers in cafes employ the 3rd person singular present indicative: "¿Usted me pone...?" with the subject omitted. It translates literally as "Does your honor put/serve me...", radiating warm colloquial politeness.

pronunciation.title: Alveolar Tap /ɾ/ & Syllable Blending
pronunciation.text: Notice the liaison in «pone un»: the vowel [e] links seamlessly into [u] without glottal hesitation: /po-newn/. Soft dental fricative on -do [ðo].

mnemonic.title: Stress on «a-VE-na»
mnemonic.text: Put the weight on the middle syllable, «a-VE-na», and let the last one fall away.

grammar.title: Plural «Tienen» vs «Hay»
grammar.text: Addressing the establishment as a plural entity (ustedes) is the most natural, welcoming way to ask stock availability in Spain and Latin America without sounding overly direct.

pronunciation.title: Bilabial Approximant [β̞] in «avena»
pronunciation.text: Spanish «v» in avena sounds identical to a soft «b» between vowels: lips do not touch completely, producing smooth airflow without English teeth friction.

mnemonic.title: Air Pen Scribble Gesture
mnemonic.text: Catch the waiter's eye across the terrace, subtly trace an invisible signature in the air while uttering: «La CUEN-ta».

grammar.title: Definite Article in Request
grammar.text: Always use the definite article «la» (never indefinite «una cuenta») because the bill for this table is specific and unique.

pronunciation.title: Diphthong /we/ in «cuenta»
pronunciation.text: The «cue-» produces an explosive glide /kw/. Stress falls punchily on [KWEHN], releasing softly onto [tah].

native.text: Can we sit outside on the terrace?

mnemonic.title: Sunlit Terrace Pivot
mnemonic.text: Glance toward the sunny sidewalk umbrellas. The prompt starts with a featherweight whisper: «se puede» ("is it permitted").

grammar.title: Impersonal «Se» of Permission
grammar.text: «¿Se puede...?» replaces "Can I / Can we", making inquiries sound polite and unpresumptuous. The main verb sentarse (to sit) is colloquially elided.

pronunciation.title: Castilian «z» [θ] and trilled «rr»
pronunciation.text: In Castilian Spanish, the «z» in terraza is articulated with the tongue between teeth as [θ] (like "thin"), preceded by a vivid double-r roll.

mnemonic.title: Clear Stop Cue
mnemonic.text: Emphasize the crisp, sharp «Sin» to clearly signal dietary necessity to the barista before the milk is poured.

grammar.title: Prepositional Modifier «Sin»
grammar.text: In Spanish gastronomy, «sin» modifies beverages and dishes without requiring the article (e.g. «sin azúcar», «sin lactosa», «sin gluten»).

pronunciation.title: Penultimate Stress on «GLU-ten»
pronunciation.text: Spanish stresses the first syllable «GLU-ten» with a pure Spanish /u/ vowel, contrasting with English elongation /ɡluːtən/.

native.text: A properly poured draft beer, boss

mnemonic.title: Foam Crown Visualizer
mnemonic.text: Notice the rhythm on «bien ti-RA-da». A caña in Madrid must have a creamy two-finger foam crown (giste).

grammar.title: Vocative «Jefe» in Bar Madrid
grammar.text: Addressing the bartender as «jefe» (boss) or «compañero» signals seasoned local fluency and immediate warmth without being impudent.

pronunciation.title: Palatal Nasal /ɲ/ in «caña»
pronunciation.text: Arch of the tongue presses smoothly against hard palate for the ñ sound, followed by crisp non-aspirated /k/.
